title: Show HN: I got tired of travel spreadsheets so I made a travel planner app
author: stavros
body: Hey everyone! I couldn't find an app to organize trips that gave me all the info I wanted to schedule each stop per day, with travel times, leeway, etc, so I made Wherewhen.The basic differentiator is that you can set various constraints (e.g. "I want to spend 2 hours in the park", or "I have a dinner reservation at 6"), and Wherewhen will automatically adjust the rest of the times to tell you when to go/leave each place, including travel.I've tried to make it mobile-friendly but travel planning is pretty complicated and it's a bit clunky on mobile.Feedback is appreciated!

title: Show HN: MealWords – Show waiters what you can't eat, in their language
author: LewisOrton
body: Last month I went to Indonesia, and was eating at a local place with friends who did not eat raw fish&green onions. We tried ChatGPT (of course) it worked, except it wasnt a smooth experience: taking too long, and difficult for the staff to provide proper feedback quickly.Then I realized I only needed to tell the waiter what we won't eat, and ask for recommendations, that's all. So I made MealWords (recommend to try on your phone):1. You pick allergies, dietary and preferences in your language (peanuts, no cilantro, not spicy etc) and it shows the card in the staff's language.2. The waiter taps anything they can't do on the card, or just confirms. You read the answer in your own language.On translations: nothing is machine-translated (well, llm-assisted for research but not mechanical translations). For allergens&terms I used all official guidance I could find (FDA, EFSA, Japan etc all official governments and local public health orgs) to make sure I used not only accurate but also understandable terms. Then I worked with native speakers (aka my friends all over the world) to proofread it as plain kitchen language, NOT medical wording (if you speak one of the languages and something feels odd, I'd really like to know!) Also, wordings were carefully chosen to meet local culture (for example if the target language is Chinese, there are extra explanations about peanut allergy when chosen, and what local sauces should be avoided in Chinese, where the general are not familiar with the concept enough compared to other places like Japan)Technical bits: the website is static, no account, card and choices stay in the browser (page analytics etc are described on the privacy page as they are but no privacy is collected)

# cu1ch3n/papilot

A Cursor-like workspace for your papers: annotate and review PDFs directly without ever touching LaTeX.

- academic-writing

## README

 

 
 
 
 

 Papilot 

 A Cursor-like workspace for your papers: annotate and review PDFs directly without ever touching LaTeX. 

 English · 简体中文 

CI
npm
License: MIT
Node.js
TypeScript
React
LaTeX
PRs welcome

Codex
Claude
Antigravity

 

 

 

 

You read and mark up the PDF the way a supervisor marks up a draft. An AI agent makes the edits in LaTeX, and every change comes back to you as a before-and-after of the typeset page. Nothing touches your paper until you accept it.

## ✨ Features

 
 
 
 
 📝 Mark up the PDF 
Select a sentence or circle an equation and say what should change. SyncTeX hands the agent the exact LaTeX lines.
 
 
 
 ✅ Approve change by change 
Each edit comes back as a typeset diff. Accept, reject or comment on it, and undo any decision.
 
 
 
 
 
 📖 Read it like a real PDF 
Jump to any section from the contents, search every page and zoom in sharply. Selecting text picks exactly the printed words.
 
 
 
 🌿 Commit when you're happy 
Diff files and commit the ones you choose, with a commit message an agent writes. Pull and push, or merge a coauthor's changes and let an agent resolve the conflicts.
 
 
 

Also: ✨ **skills** such as Polish, Proofread and Check math, one `/` away, plus your own · 🤖 **Codex, Claude or Antigravity**, each with your own login · 🌳 **every task in its own Git worktree**, up to two at once · 🌗 **light and dark** · 📱 **runs on your computer**, and you can open it from your phone.

## 🚀 Quick start

> [!NOTE]
> You need **Node.js 22.22+**, **Git** and a full **TeX** distribution (MacTeX or TeX Live). Revising also needs one signed-in agent.

```sh
npm install -g papilot
papilot demo
```

Open **http://127.0.0.1:7274** and choose **PDF** in the sidebar. The demo adds an example paper to revise: a 26-page LaTeX paper about Papilot itself, full of equations. When you are ready, run `papilot` and choose **Add paper** to add any LaTeX project in a Git repository.

## 🤖 Agents

| Agent | Sign in once | How Papilot runs it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Codex** | `papilot codex login` | Through the Codex app server, in its workspace sandbox. Papilot uses your `codex` if you have one, or installs it on first start. |
| **Claude** | Start `papilot` with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` set | Through the Claude Agent SDK, downloaded the first time. The SDK does not accept a Pro or Max subscription login. |
| **Antigravity** | Install Antigravity and sign in to `agy` | `agy -p`, one process per turn, editing files only. If your region needs it, set `PAPILOT_AGY_PROXY`. |

Papilot never reads, stores or forwards your credentials. An agent that isn't installed or signed in shows as unavailable.

Having trouble getting started? Run `papilot doctor` for environment checks and fixes, or `papilot doctor --repo /path/to/paper` to check a paper too. Add `--json` for a machine-readable report. Diagnostics do not install software, start the server or change your paper. See the diagnostics guide for what is checked.

 
 ⚙️ Options and remote access 

 

```sh
papilot --port 4400            # another local port
papilot --data ~/papilot-data  # keep state somewhere else (default ~/.papilot)
papilot service install        # macOS: start after login, restart if it exits
npm uninstall -g papilot       # remove it; your state stays in ~/.papilot until you delete it
```

Papilot listens only on `127.0.0.1`. To use it from another device, publish it on your tailnet with Tailscale Serve and set `PAPILOT_PUBLIC_ORIGIN` and `PAPILOT_TAILSCALE_LOGIN`. Papilot then checks the host, the browser origin and the Tailscale identity of every request. The guide has the steps.

 

 
 🛠️ Develop 

 

```sh
git clone https://github.com/cu1ch3n/papilot && cd papilot
npm ci && npm run setup:review
npm run build && npm start
```

Run `npm run typecheck`, `npm test` and `npm run test:ui` before sending a pull request.

 

## 📚 Documentation

The **guide** covers every part of the workspace, the configuration variables, recovery after restarts, and development. The example paper in `examples/papilot-paper` explains the design in depth, with proofs. What changed in each release is in the changelog.

## 💬 Community

- 💡 **Questions and ideas**: Discussions
- 🐛 **Something broke**: open an issue
- 🤝 **Want to help**: pick a good first issue and read CONTRIBUTING.md

If Papilot saves you time on a paper, a ⭐ helps other researchers find it.

Hello all,Ive been building Fabivo, a free furniture planner that runs in the browser. You sketch it simply by drawing it, (by far my favorite feature of this app), clicking for boards or just selecting some starting designs.But what i think separates fabivo from others its the image to model ai assistant, which took me a looong time to develop and get some quirks fixed, thanks god latest models are focusing on 3d, thats been helping too!The photo part is an image to JSON CAD harness: the model returns a parametric furniture model in mm that the app can build and edit. That harness is also what i benchmark, and honestly its the reason the app exists. I wanted to see if a photo could turn into a plan i could take to the saw.Also finetuned some image models and found interesting stuff, that was a first. My intention was to basically reuse the drawing feature to convert a 2d line sketch from image models like gpt image / nano banana to my parametric model, which "worked", and was actually thinking of using that for prod, but then cheaper/better models at 3d launched, but anyways, i learned a lot!Im getting better performance from my harness than from plain 3js, tho this is anecdotally and havent actually benchmarked it...Happy to answer anything, especially about the harness or the cut order.edit: Adding the numbers, missed them.17 photos of real furniture, three models, same harness, medium reasoning, same tools. Scored on how close the returned structure and boards are to the gold model, so its my own set. ## README

# Local Code

Local Code is a private AI agent for Mac, iPad and iPhone, written mostly in Swift. It puts three things in one app: an LLM inference engine for Apple Silicon, a coding harness tuned to each model, and an agent runtime with Python, Node.js, a shell and other familiar tools built in. With these, the agent can work through whole tasks on files you choose, such as analyzing data, charting it, writing documents and slide decks, or building software.

With an on-device quasi-frontier model, such as DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017, inference runs on your device and works offline. You can also pick a cloud model from Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter or an OpenAI-compatible server. When you do, your prompts, file contents and tool output go to that provider. Either way, the agent's tools run inside the app's sandbox and can reach only the folders you allow.

Download Local Code from getlocalcode.app.

This repository contains the source code of the app and its command-line tools, along with the libraries and vendored dependencies they are built from.

## An Agent That Does Real Work

An agent that does real work needs more than an inference engine, a harness and a model. It also needs what people expect from well-made software:

- **Durable tasks and threads:** tasks and chat threads are saved, so you can close the app and pick them up later.
- **Resumable generation:** an interrupted reply, reasoning included, continues where it stopped instead of starting over.
- **Steering:** you can send a message at any time, even while the agent is working, to change its course.
- **Long-term context cache:** the model's context is saved to disk, including images and the recurrent state that some models keep, so a long conversation isn't read again from the start.

The engine and the model still matter, and the rest of this section covers them: the models, the sandbox the agent works in, and how fast and how accurately the models run.

### Models

Local Code downloads its own quantized checkpoints of each model:

| Model | Quantizations | Input | Download size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 | 2-bit S, 3-bit S | Text and images | 376 GB, 412 GB |
| DeepSeek 4 Flash 0731 | 2-bit S | Text | 89.4 GB |
| Qwen 3.8 27B | 2-bit S, 4-bit S, 8-bit S | Text and images | 9.6 GB, 21.3 GB, 29.2 GB |

The DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 sizes include a 203 GB engram file, which both of its quantizations share.

The DeepSeek models are mixtures of experts, and they are larger than the memory of most Macs. For example, the DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 (2-bit S) checkpoint is about 173 GB. Local Code keeps as many of the most used experts in memory as there is room for, and streams the rest from disk. It also leaves room for the other apps you run. The experts kept in memory never take more than the Mac's memory minus 32 GB, or more than 72% of the memory that is free when the model loads. So these models run on Macs with less memory than the checkpoint, run faster the more memory there is, and leave the rest of the Mac usable.

During setup, Local Code suggests a model based on the device's memory:

- under 32 GB: Qwen 3.8 27B (2-bit S)
- 32 GB and up: Qwen 3.8 27B (4-bit S)
- 48 GB and up: DeepSeek 4 Flash 0731
- 64 GB and up: DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017

You can switch to any model later.

### The In-App Sandbox

Local Code doesn't run the agent's commands as separate programs on your computer. The shell, the language runtimes and the command-line tools are compiled into the app and run in its own process, inside Apple's App Sandbox. On a Mac, the Hardened Runtime also protects the app's code. The agent has no full-disk access, and it can't launch other programs on your computer, so it can't run native programs that aren't built into the app.

Each project is a folder inside a workspace that you choose. The agent starts in the project folder and can read and write anywhere in the workspace, plus the app's temporary folder. Packages and caches that the agent installs for a project stay in that project's folder. Commands that use the network, such as web search, `curl` and `ssh`, connect out when the agent runs them.

The sandbox includes:

- **Shell:** OSH from Oils, with common Unix commands such as `grep`, `sed`, `awk`, `find`, `diff`, `rg`, `jq`, `zip`, `curl`, `git` and `ssh`.
- **Python 3.14:** NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, Pillow, lxml, openpyxl, python-docx, python-pptx and pypdf, and `pip` for more.
- **Node.js 24:** `npm` and `npx`.
- **Lean 4 and Z3:** to check proofs and solve constraint problems. Lean can also install Mathlib.
- **Documents and media:** LibreOffice, through the `office` command, to convert and render Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF files. Also FFmpeg, plus `html2video` and `hyperframes` to make videos from HTML.
- **Web:** web search, and a WebKit browser that the agent can drive to test pages or to use sites that need JavaScript or a sign-in.
- **Images and video:** the Draw Things CLI, to generate images and videos.
- **Personal data:** `calendar` to read and edit events, and `photos` to find, import, edit and organize photos and videos. On a Mac, `notes`, `mail` and `imessage` also read Notes, Mail and Messages, but they can't change or send anything. Each command works only after you grant access.

Built-in skills show the agent how to use these tools for common work:

| Skill | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `office` | Create, read, edit and check Word, PowerPoint and Excel files and CSV or TSV tables, and export them to PDF or images |
| `answers-charts` | Draw data charts with Python and Matplotlib, shown inline in the answer |
| `hyperframes` | Make motion graphics and timed HTML compositions, such as animated text, captions and slideshows, and render them to video |
| `use-draw-things-cli` | Generate and edit images, and create videos, with the Draw Things CLI |
| `use-web-browse-cli` | Drive the WebKit browser to test pages, or to use sites that need JavaScript or a sign-in |
| `deploy-static-site-with-wrangler` | Publish a folder of static web files to a temporary public URL with Cloudflare Wrangler |
| `use-mcp-with-mcporter` | Connect to Model Context Protocol servers and call their tools through MCPorter |
| `check_lean-and-lean-tools` | Prove non-obvious claims about code, such as ones about recursive functions or data structures, with Lean |
| `skill-creator` | Create, import, update and validate skills |
| `introduce-local-code` | Explain what Local Code is and what the agent can do |

You can add your own skills to a project's `.agents/skills` folder.

### Performance on Macs

Speeds are in tokens per second, given as prefill / decode. Each column starts with that much context already in use. On top of it, Local Code prefills one more full chunk, and separately decodes 128 tokens. A chunk is the most Local Code prefills at once on that Mac: 4,096 tokens on the M5 Max, and 8,192 on the M5 Ultra.

**M5 Max, 128 GB**

| Model | 8K already in context | 16K already in context | 32K already in context | 128K already in context |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen 3.8 27B (4-bit S) | 1,450 / 40.4 | 1,296 / 35.0 | 1,005 / 27.9 | 456 / 13.5 |
| DeepSeek 4 Flash 0731 (2-bit S) | 1,361 / 42.3 | 1,316 / 41.7 | 1,237 / 40.9 | 924 / 36.7 |
| DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 (2-bit S) | 346 / 18.7 | 339 / 17.1 | 339 / 17.2 | 355 / 15.7 |

On the M5 Max, the DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 readings set Weights Streaming to 56 GiB (`--weights-streaming 56` in the CLI). DeepSeek 4 Flash 0731 keeps all of its weights in memory.

**M5 Ultra, 256 GB**

| Model | 8K already in context | 16K already in context | 32K already in context | 128K already in context |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen 3.8 27B (4-bit S) | 2,689 / 54.5 | 2,247 / 44.0 | 1,988 / 33.2 | 962 / 12.2 |
| DeepSeek 4 Flash 0731 (2-bit S) | 3,384 / 56.2 | 3,265 / 55.9 | 3,039 / 54.7 | 2,087 / 50.4 |
| DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 (2-bit S) | 4,600 / 58.9 | 4,507 / 58.6 | 4,431 / 57.9 | 3,840 / 56.1 |

On the M5 Ultra, both DeepSeek readings are a second pass in the same session, without the 20-second cool-down before each prefill. For DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017, its engram entries are also already in memory.

This chart compares DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 prefill speed on the same M5 Ultra in Local Code, in MLX-Serve v26.10.3 with the iQ-MLX 3.0bpw checkpoint, and in oMLX 0.7.2 with the oQ2.5e checkpoint. Each reading times only the prefill of an 8,192-token chunk on top of the given amount of context. The Local Code readings come from the same runs as the table above, and the MLX-Serve and oMLX readings, both with CED on, are medians of three runs. The label above each Local Code point is how much faster it is than the faster of MLX-Serve and oMLX at that context length.

 
 
 
 

 
 Data 

Speeds are in tokens per second.

| Context in use | Local Code (2-bit S) | MLX-Serve v26.10.3 (iQ-MLX 3.0bpw) | oMLX 0.7.2 (oQ2.5e) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 4,547 | 1,945 | 1,529 |
| 8K | 4,600 | 1,900 | 1,653 |
| 16K | 4,507 | 1,706 | 1,615 |
| 32K | 4,431 | 1,217 | 1,558 |
| 128K | 3,840 | 1,087 | 1,335 |

 

To measure your own Mac, open Model Speed in the app, or run the same measurements, at context lengths up to the model's limit, with the CLI:

```bash
bazel run -c opt //Apps/LocalCode:LocalCodeCLI -- speedometer \
  --model qwen_3.8_27b_i4x.ckpt --result-json /path/to/speed.json
```

### Benchmarks

This chart compares DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 (2-bit S) in Local Code with the scores DeepSeek reported for DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 0910:

 
 
 
 

| Benchmark | DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 0910 (as reported) | DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 0910 (2-bit S) | DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 (2-bit S) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AIME 2026 | — | 30/30 (100%) | 30/30 (100%) |
| MathArena Apex | 65.6% | 7/12 (58.3%) | 10.3/12 (86.1%) |
| GPQA Diamond | 90.9% | 179/198 (90.4%) | 185/198 (93.4%) |

Reported scores are from the model card, at maximum reasoning effort. The 2-bit S MathArena Apex scores average several runs of its 12 problems: two for 0910 and three for 1017.

Average reasoning tokens per attempt:

| Benchmark | DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 0910 (as reported) | DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 0910 (2-bit S) | DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 (2-bit S) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AIME 2026 | — | 15,710 | 16,909 |
| MathArena Apex | — | 161,725 | 120,657 |
| GPQA Diamond | — | 31,042 | 22,103 |

### Quantization Quality

KL divergence (KLD) measures how far a quantized model's predictions drift from the original model's. Lower is closer. These charts compare the KLD of DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 quantizations against the size of their weights, on two datasets: Wiki10k, and conversation traces (only assistant tokens).

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 

Sizes leave out the engram table and the MTP layers. The checkpoints store the engram table at different precisions, and only the MLX checkpoints include MTP layers.

 
 Data 

| Checkpoint | Size of weights | KLD, Wiki10k | KLD, conversation traces (only assistant tokens) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Local Code 2-bit S | 173.0 GB | 0.28516 | 0.050512 |
| Local Code 3-bit S | 209.6 GB | 0.18850 | 0.027868 |
| Unsloth UD-IQ2_XXS | 165.3 GB | 0.23621 | 0.034424 |
| Unsloth UD-Q2_K_XL | 199.6 GB | 0.14755 | 0.021310 |
| MLX-Serve iQ-MLX 3.0bpw | 213.9 GB | 0.20453 | 0.045695 |
| oMLX oQ2.5e | 211.5 GB | 0.26888 | 0.045604 |
| oMLX oQ3e | 248.6 GB | 0.13462 | 0.021685 |

 

### Qwen 3.8 27B

Qwen 3.8 27B is a small model that understands images, and it is strong at coding and long-horizon work. Local Code suggests it for devices with less than 48 GB of memory.

#### Prefill Speed

Before a model writes its first token, it has to read the whole prompt. For an agent, that means the conversation so far, the files it has opened and the output of its tools. This step is called prefill. Each tool call adds to the context, so in agent work, prefill is often what you wait for.

The chart compares prefill speed in Local Code and in Splash, an open-source inference engine for Apple silicon, on an M5 Ultra with 256 GB of memory. Splash runs the model's UD-Q4_K_XL GGUF checkpoint. Each reading prefills an 8,192-token chunk after the given amount of context is already in use. The label above each Local Code point is how much faster it is than the faster of the two Splash settings.

 
 
 
 

 
 Data 

Speeds are in tokens per second.

| Context in use | Local Code (4-bit S) | Splash (BF16 KV cache) | Splash (Int8 KV cache) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 3,048 | 1,897 | 1,896 |
| 8K | 2,689 | 1,747 | 1,749 |
| 16K | 2,247 | 1,596 | 1,621 |
| 32K | 1,988 | 1,364 | 1,406 |
| 64K | 1,485 | 1,065 | 1,112 |
| 128K | 962 | 710 | 778 |

 

Splash decodes faster than Local Code because it drafts tokens with the DFlash2 draft model. This comparison leaves decode out, because it compares how the two engines implement attention.

#### Why Local Code Prefills Faster

As the context grows, the extra prefill time goes to attention. For each new token, attention does two large matrix multiplications against every earlier token:

- **QK:** the new token's query (Q) is multiplied with the key (K) of each earlier token, which scores how relevant that token is.
- **PV:** those scores (P) are used to take a weighted sum of the earlier tokens' values (V).

Both grow with the length of the context, so at 64K or 128K tokens they take a large share of the prefill time.

The GPUs in Apple's M5 chips and later multiply two Int8 matrices faster than they multiply floating-point ones. Local Code converts both Q and K to Int8, so QK runs at that faster rate. It computes PV in floating point.

Splash's default Int8 KV cache also stores K and V in Int8, but it multiplies them with BF16 numbers in both QK and PV. Because one side of each multiplication is BF16, Splash can't use the faster Int8 × Int8 path. The Int8 cache saves memory, and makes long-context prefill only a little faster, by 10% at 128K. Local Code is still 24% faster there.

#### Accuracy

The faster attention doesn't cost accuracy on long inputs. On a 150-question subset of LongBench v2, Local Code's 4-bit S checkpoint scores within one question of Splash, with either KV cache:

| Engine | LongBench v2 (150-question subset) |
| --- | --- |
| Local Code, 4-bit S | 106/150 (70.7%) |
| Splash, BF16 KV cache | 107/150 (71.3%) |
| Splash, Int8 KV cache | 107/150 (71.3%) |

## Repository Layout

| Path | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `Apps/LocalCode` | The app, and `LocalCodeCLI`, which runs the app's agents on macOS (CLI/README.md) |
| `Apps/DrawThingsCLI`, `Apps/HTML2VideoCLI`, `Apps/HyperFramesCLI` | Commands that are available in the agent's shell and as standalone macOS executables |
| `Libraries` | Swift libraries for model inference (`SwiftLLM`, `SwiftDiffusion`), the model catalog (`LLMZoo`), the agent's shell (`BashToolContext`), and the rest of the app |
| `Vendors` | Third-party code, plus prebuilt Python, Node.js and LibreOffice frameworks |
| `Scripts`, `Tools` | Setup, formatting, packaging and release scripts |

The neural network runtime, s4nnc, and the other external dependencies are pinned in `WORKSPACE.darwin`.

## Building

Local Code builds on macOS with Xcode and Bazel. The Bazel version is pinned in `.bazelversion`, which Bazelisk reads automatically.

The prebuilt Python, Node.js and LibreOffice frameworks under `Vendors/` are stored with Git LFS. Install Git LFS before you clone, or fetch the files afterward:

```bash
git lfs install
git lfs pull
```

Then set up the checkout once:

```bash
./Scripts/install.sh
```

The script installs the swift-format and buildifier pre-commit hooks, writes a `.bazelrc` that imports `.bazelrc.darwin`, links `WORKSPACE` to `WORKSPACE.darwin`, and installs `coreutils` and `cmake` with Homebrew. If you only need to build, the two Bazel steps are enough:

```bash
ln -s WORKSPACE.darwin WORKSPACE
echo 'try-import %workspace%/.bazelrc.darwin' > .bazelrc
```

Use a link instead of a copy for `WORKSPACE`, so that it stays current when dependency pins in `WORKSPACE.darwin` change.

Machine-specific flags go in `.bazelrc.local`, which `.bazelrc.darwin` imports and Git ignores. Xcode 27 no longer includes `ld-classic`, which FFmpeg and Lean need, so with Xcode 27 point the build at the copy in an Xcode 26 installation:

```
build --action_env="FFMPEG_LD_CLASSIC=/Applications/Xcode 26.6.app/Contents/Developer/Toolchains/XcodeDefault.xctoolchain/usr/bin/ld-classic"
build --define="LEAN_LD_CLASSIC=/Applications/Xcode 26.6.app/Contents/Developer/Toolchains/XcodeDefault.xctoolchain/usr/bin/ld-classic"
```

Build the app for iPhone and iPad:

```bash
bazel build //Apps/LocalCode:LocalCode --ios_multi_cpus=arm64
```

Add `--config=release` for an optimized build. A device build needs a provisioning profile, and this repository doesn't include one. Put your own development profile at `Apps/LocalCode/ProvisioningFiles/LocalCode_Development.mobileprovision`, and change `bundle_id` in `Apps/LocalCode/BUILD` to that profile's app ID. If your team can't use the Sign in with Apple and associated domains entitlements, also remove them from `Apps/LocalCode/SupportingFiles/LocalCode.entitlements`.

The Mac app is a Mac Catalyst build that needs a patched version of Bazel, which isn't published yet. On a Mac, you can run the same agents with `LocalCodeCLI`, which needs no signing:

```bash
bazel run //Apps/LocalCode:LocalCodeCLI -- models
bazel run //Apps/LocalCode:LocalCodeCLI -- local-agent \
  --model qwen_3.8_27b_i4x.ckpt --project /path/to/project \
  --message 'Review the parser and fix the failing tests.'
```

See Apps/LocalCode/CLI/README.md for remote providers, sign-in, saving and resuming runs, and benchmarks.

## Repository Sync

Local Code is developed in the private Draw Things mono-repository. Each commit there that touches a path listed in SYNCLIST is applied to this repository. Each line of `SYNCLIST` is either a path that has the same name in both repositories, or `private path -> path here` when the names differ. A line that starts with `!` leaves a path out. For example, `!Apps/LocalCode/ProvisioningFiles` keeps the team's provisioning profiles out of this repository.

Files that are not listed in `SYNCLIST`, such as this README, `LICENSE.md`, `Apps/BUILD`, `force_sync.sh` and `.github/`, are maintained in this repository only.

Commits made here can also be applied back to the private repository by cross-repo-synchronization.yaml. That direction is turned off for now, so the workflow runs only when it is started by hand.

## README

# LFM3 video chat

Talk to LFM3-Omni-2B through your
microphone and camera. The model replies with text and audio, and you can
interrupt it by speaking or pressing a button.

Start the server and open http://localhost:8000 on the same computer.
Camera and microphone access on localhost works without SSL certificates.

An ONNX version is available in `src-onnx/`, with a separate
uv environment. Use `q4` for CPU or `q4f16` for NVIDIA GPU. It supports the same
camera, voice, and interruption controls without installing PyTorch.

To download ONNX weights separately, use the bundle download commands.

## Get started

You need uv and a microphone. The project uses Python
3.12. Run these commands from the project folder on the computer hosting the model.

Install the dependencies:

```bash
uv sync
```

Already downloaded the model? Skip the next command and use your existing folder
with `--model`. Otherwise, download it once:

```bash
uv run hf download LiquidAI/LFM3-Omni-2B --local-dir resources/models/lfm3-omni-2b
```

Start the chat, replacing the model path if needed:

```bash
uv run serve --model resources/models/lfm3-omni-2b
```

Open http://localhost:8000 on the same computer. HTTPS is not needed for localhost.
The server uses existing model files by default; `--download` allows it to fetch
missing files. If your model is already in the Hugging Face cache, you can omit
`--model`.

## Have a conversation

1. Click **Start conversation** and allow microphone and camera access.
2. Speak, then pause for a reply. Audio plays as the model generates it.
3. Speak over a reply to interrupt it, or click **Interrupt & speak**. Headphones
 help prevent speaker echo from causing unwanted interruptions.
4. Open **Conversation settings** to turn camera sharing or hands-free speech on
 or off, or adjust the microphone threshold.
5. Click **End** to stop the camera and microphone. **Start fresh** clears the
 conversation history.

The assistant begins answering after your turn ends. It does not generate an
answer while you are still speaking.

## Pause to think with Smart Turn

Smart Turn v3.2 helps distinguish a thinking pause from the end of a sentence.
To enable it and download any missing model files on the first run:

```bash
uv run serve \
  --model resources/models/lfm3-omni-2b \
  --turn-detector smart --download
```

After that, omit `--download`. The default `auto` setting uses Smart Turn when it
is available locally and falls back to silence detection otherwise. You can
choose silence detection explicitly with `--turn-detector silence`.

Smart Turn runs on the CPU. It gives you time to continue an unfinished thought,
with a short silence timeout so the conversation does not stay waiting forever.
You can always press **Send** to finish your turn immediately.

Its model is kept in `resources/models/smart-turn-v3/`. Keep that folder to reuse
the download. Deleting it removes the local model copy. For an existing ONNX file,
use `--turn-model /path/to/smart-turn-v3.2-cpu.onnx`.

## Connect from another device

To connect from another device, use HTTPS for camera and microphone access.
Start the server with `--host 0.0.0.0` to accept local network connections.
This setup is optional; local use on http://localhost:8000 needs no certificate.

Use a certificate trusted by the connecting device. For development, you can
create a self-signed certificate. Replace ` ` below with your server's
LAN address before running the command:

```bash
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 365 \
  -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -subj "/CN=localhost" \
  -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:localhost,IP:127.0.0.1,IP:<server-ip>"
chmod 600 key.pem
```

Then run:

```bash
uv run serve \
  --model resources/models/lfm3-omni-2b \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --ssl-certfile cert.pem \
  --ssl-keyfile key.pem
```

Trust the certificate on the connecting device, then open
https://:8000/ there. The browser automatically uses a secure WebSocket
for audio and video frames. If the page cannot connect, check that the server's
firewall allows your chosen port.

Both certificate flags are required together. `cert.pem` and `key.pem` are
ignored by Git. Keep the private key private.

## Development checks and preview

Run the local tests:

```bash
uv run pytest
node --test tests/test-turn-gate.cjs
```

Preview the interface without loading LFM3 weights:

```bash
uv run --python 3.12 tests/live_fixture.py --port 8001
```

Open http://localhost:8001. The preview is labelled and uses fixed text, synthetic
audio, and scripted turn decisions. It demonstrates the interface and interaction
flow, not the model's response quality or speed.

To check loading and inference of the real Smart Turn model:

```bash
uv run --python 3.12 tests/check_smart_turn.py
```

This check downloads the classifier if missing and tests it on silence. It does
not measure accuracy on real speech. On their first run, `uv` may also install the
check scripts' Python dependencies.

Both scripts are saved under `tests/`. Downloaded model assets are kept under
`resources/`, which is ignored by Git. Your own LFM3 folder can be anywhere; pass
its path with `--model`.

title: Show HN: I built a tool that finds reliability bugs in your code
author: aray07
body: Hey HN,I’m Abhishek. I'm building Opslane, a tool that finds reliability issues in your code. On every PR, it spins up your entire app and then tries to find weak spots that would break in production.Demo: https://youtu.be/47phxkdh6f0Example: We tested Opslane on Lago (open-source billing) and found a bug where customers get double charged. Opslane made Stripe take the money and then return a 500. Lago marked the payment failed. A retry from the dashboard charged the customer again. https://github.com/getlago/lago-api/issues/6903Why I built thisI used to work on reliability at Robinhood. We used to run chaos testing in our staging environments: inject faults in various parts of the system and see what breaks. We found issues like Kafka or Redis being unavailable for a few seconds could take the whole app down.But that kind of testing was expensive. It needed a well maintained staging environment. Engineers needed to know what to test. Most teams never actually did it.Over the last year, coding agents have gone writing some of my code to almost all my code now. Teams are shipping way more code than they were 6 months ago.Code review tools read the diff, but a lot of reliability bugs aren't in the diff. They're in how your code behaves when Stripe, Redis or the network misbehaves. And e2e tests usually mock those services out and test the happy path.Agents have made this type of testing a lot cheaper. And we will see more of this (kinda like security scanning / testing)How it worksA full copy of your app per PR: Postgres, Redis, Kafka, SQS, S3.Working copies of your third-party dependencies: Stripe, Slack, Gmail and more. Traffic goes through our proxy, which lets us inject failures.The agent picks what to test: It reads every PR and writes down invariants that need to hold (for e.g. a customer should never be charged twice). It then injects faults likely to break the invariants.Bugs we've foundWe ran Opslane on some popular open-source apps and here are some of the bugs we have found:1/ Twenty: deleting a workspace while Stripe is failing locks everyone out, and billing keeps going. Twenty merged a fix. (https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/issues/28043)2/ Dub: a restart in the middle of a payout paid a partner $240 for $120 owed. (https://github.com/dubinc/dub.link/issues/4707)Full list: opslane.com/open-sourceOpslane is pretty early - we have a couple of early customers. We have found bugs in their system that their other code review tools missed.Would love to get feedback from folks and how they are seeing the reliability of their systems evolve over time with agents.

# kavachlabs/kavach

Replay the crash. Prove the fix. 81ns in-process flight recorder, 61µs deterministic replay, and 5.9ms variant fix verification for journal-driven services and AI coding agents.

- Stars: 0
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 0
- Open issues: 1
- License: Apache License 2.0
- Homepage: https://www.thekavachlabs.com
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-06T13:58:52Z

## Languages

- C
- C++
- CMake
- CSS
- Dockerfile
- Dune
- Elixir
- Go
- HTML
- Haskell
- Java
- JavaScript
- Julia
- OCaml
- PHP
- Python
- Ruby
- Rust
- Shell
- TypeScript

## Topics

- claude-code
- coding-agents
- debugging
- deterministic-simulation-testing
- event-sourcing
- fault-injection
- golang
- mcp
- mcp-server
- property-based-testing
- python
- replay
- rust
- testing
- typescript

## Top Contributors

- eulerkochy (272 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 
 
 
 

ci
sdk
release
codecov

**Replay the crash. Prove the fix.**

Kavach records every input, clock read, and random read a service makes. When a step panics, returns an error, or breaks a declared invariant, it flushes a compact `.kavach` fixture that replays byte for byte in microseconds—with no broker, database, or network—and rejects narrow patches that fail across perturbed variants of the incident.

| Metric | Measured | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recorder overhead per event (shared-memory ring) | **81.2 ns** | Median of 5 runs (BENCHMARKS.md) |
| Full incident replay, in-process | **61.1 µs** | 33 records, 8 steps, 2 invariants/step |
| Fix verification across 56 variants, in-process | **5.9 ms** | `kavach diff` (`196.4 ms` end-to-end across 105 binary runs) |
| Narrow single-event fixes rejected | **10 / 10** | Ten planted bugs in `bench/`, `1,000 / 1,000` byte-identical replays |

**Scope:** deterministic replay, variant fix verification, and contract-first feature verification for single-writer, journal-driven services in **12 languages** (sdk) or over two small wire protocols (INTEGRATING.md). Explore multi-arm coding agent runs on real open-source incidents at benchmark.kavachlabs.dev.

> **Status: pre-alpha.** The journal format (SPEC.md), the flight
> recorder, replay and the CLI work on the demo service. APIs and the format
> will change before 1.0. Every performance number this project publishes is in
> BENCHMARKS.md with the command that measured it.

## Install

Install prebuilt `kavach` and `kavach-recorder` binaries **plus all four Kavach agent skills** on Linux or macOS (`amd64` / `arm64`) in a single command (no Go toolchain required):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://www.thekavachlabs.com/install.sh | sh
```

Or install only the agent skills via `npx skills`, or build the CLI from source with Go 1.24+:

```bash
npx skills add kavachlabs/kavach
go install github.com/kavachlabs/kavach/cmd/kavach@latest
go install github.com/kavachlabs/kavach/cmd/kavach-recorder@latest
```

## Try it

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 1080p 60fps video:
 Hero cut (dark, 0:24) ·
 Hero cut (light, 0:24) ·
 Full walkthrough (dark, 0:47) ·
 Full walkthrough (light, 0:47) 
 
 

The demo is a wallet ledger that crashes when upstream sends `"amount": null`.
The commands below use its Go version; every SDK under sdk has a port
with the same bug. The CLI and the recorder are written in Go, so building them
from source needs Go; your service does not.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kavachlabs/kavach && cd kavach
go install ./cmd/kavach ./cmd/kavach-recorder   # or use install.sh above
go build -o ledger-old ./examples/ledger/sdk
go build -tags ledgerfix -o ledger-new ./examples/ledger/sdk   # the fixed build
go build -tags ledgerpartialfix -o ledger-partial ./examples/ledger/sdk  # a fix that is too narrow

./ledger-old -in examples/ledger/testdata/events.jsonl     # crashes, writes kavach/fixtures/ledger-*.kavach
kavach inspect kavach/fixtures/ledger-*.kavach                 # what happened, record by record
kavach replay  kavach/fixtures/ledger-*.kavach --bin ./ledger-old # still_failing@32
kavach diff    kavach/fixtures/ledger-*.kavach --old ./ledger-old --new ./ledger-new      # fixed
kavach diff    kavach/fixtures/ledger-*.kavach --old ./ledger-old --new ./ledger-partial  # variant_failed(7)@23
```

The partial fix guards only deposits, the event type in the incident. It
passes the recorded crash, but `diff` also replays 56 variants of it, and the
old build crashes the same way on 47 of them; the partial fix crashes on 8,
starting with the same event as a `transfer`.

Replay runs no external services: the fixture holds every input, clock read and
random read the handler made.

The same demo reads from Kafka through franz-go.
The topic is the ledger's journal: on every start the service folds it from the
first offset. With a local broker (for example
`docker run -p 9092:9092 apache/kafka:3.9.0`):

```bash
./ledger-old -kafka localhost:9092 -seed examples/ledger/testdata/events.jsonl  # load the topic once
./ledger-old -kafka localhost:9092                                              # crashes at offset 0:7
```

The fixture's inputs carry their Kafka positions (`kafka:wallet-events @ 0:7`),
and it still replays with no broker running. Kafka is a dependency of the demo
only, not of the SDK.

## With an AI agent

`kavach mcp` is a Model Context Protocol
server with six tools (`kavach_list_incidents`, `kavach_replay`,
`kavach_time_travel`, `kavach_diff`, `kavach_contract_show`, and
`kavach_contract_check`) returning the same verdicts as the CLI as structured
JSON:

```bash
claude mcp add kavach -- kavach mcp
npx skills add kavachlabs/kavach
```

Kavach ships with four Agent Skills (installed automatically by `install.sh` or `npx skills add kavachlabs/kavach`):

| Skill | What it teaches your agent |
| --- | --- |
| `/kavach-fix` | Reproduce a `.kavach` crash fixture and generalize the fix until `kavach diff` returns `fixed` across all incident and regression variants. |
| `/kavach-implement` | Build a new feature contract-first: record baseline traffic, declare spec invariants, stop for human `kavach contract approve`, and iterate until `pass`. |
| `/kavach-setup` | Map state boundaries into `.kavach/plan/state-map.md`, then instrument a handler or build a `kavach-host` harness in any of the 12 language SDKs. |
| `/kavach-invariants` | Write a reviewable invariant blueprint to `.kavach/plan/invariants.md`, declare the invariants, and mutation-test each one in milliseconds with `kavach replay` and `kavach diff`. |

See AGENTS.md for the complete verdict loop and rules.

## Using it in a service

| Language | SDK |
| --- | --- |
| Go | sdk/go |
| Python | sdk/python |
| TypeScript / JavaScript | sdk/typescript |
| Rust | sdk/rust |
| Java | sdk/java |
| C and C++ | sdk/c |
| Julia | sdk/julia |
| Ruby | sdk/ruby |
| PHP | sdk/php |
| Elixir | sdk/elixir |
| Haskell | sdk/haskell |
| OCaml | sdk/ocaml |

Every SDK has the same shape:

- a **handler**, called once per input, that reads the clock, random bytes,
 gateways and config, and emits its effects, only through the env it is
 given;
- a **recorder** that wraps your consume loop: one step per input, with
 effects delivered after the step succeeds;
- a **host mode**: when the program is started with `kavach-host` as its last
 argument, it serves replays to the CLI instead of consuming.

A handler can also provide snapshots, so that fixtures start from recent state
instead of from the service's first event, and declare invariants that are
checked after every step, live and in replay. Each SDK's README shows the code.

No SDK for your language? An SDK is a wrapper over the recorder and host
protocols in SPEC.md §9 and §10; INTEGRATING.md
shows how to speak them directly.

## How it works

1. **Record.** Your handler reads time and randomness, and emits effects,
 through the env the SDK gives it for each input. The SDK writes
 everything to `kavach-recorder`, a child process that keeps the journal on
 disk and writes a fixture file when the handler panics, returns an error, or
 violates an invariant, even if the service dies in the step.
2. **Replay.** `kavach replay --bin ` runs your own
 build as a host process (`--bin ./ledger`, `--bin "python -m ledger"`,
 `--bin "node dist/main.js"`)
 and folds the recorded inputs through its handler, serving every clock,
 random, gateway and config read from the fixture. Outputs are captured as
 events, never executed, so replay touches no external system.
3. **Verify.** `kavach diff --old --new ` reports the first
 output where two builds diverge. A fix only counts when the original failure
 is gone, declared invariants hold, steps before the failure still produce
 the outputs production saw, and the fix also passes at least 10 **variants**
 of the incident: perturbed copies of the journal (fields of the failing
 event changed, events reordered, dropped or redelivered, the clock shifted)
 on which the old build fails exactly as it did in production. A fix that
 only handles the recorded event does not pass. See SPEC.md §6.1.
4. **Build features against a contract.** `kavach contract check` replays
 traffic recorded before a feature on the new build. Steps outside the
 feature must produce the recorded outputs. Feature steps must change, and
 every change is listed for review. Invariants written from the spec must
 hold, on the traffic and on variants of the feature steps. See
 SPEC.md §6.4.

## In CI (GitHub Actions)

Check `.kavach` fixtures into `testdata/` and run `kavachlabs/kavach` in pull requests to replay regression fixtures or verify a candidate fix across incident variants (writing a verdict table to the workflow summary):

```yaml
- uses: kavachlabs/kavach@v0.1.0
  with:
    fixtures: testdata/*.kavach
    old: ./service-base
    new: ./service-pr
```

## Not in scope

- Multi-writer or shared-state services. Kavach assumes one writer folds the
 journal into state.
- Record-and-replay of network traffic ("tapes"). Kavach re-derives state from
 inputs; it does not stub dependencies from recorded responses.

## Repository guide

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| SPEC.md | Journal and fixture format, and the host and recorder protocols, v0 |
| AGENTS.md | How an AI coding agent should use Kavach |
| INTEGRATING.md | Using Kavach from a language with no SDK |
| sdk | The SDKs, one per language |
| commands | Agent commands: `/kavach-implement` |
| action.yml | Composite GitHub Action for `kavach replay` and `kavach diff` in CI |
| scripts/install.sh | Zero-dependency installer for Linux and macOS (`amd64` / `arm64`) |
| llms.txt | Index of these docs for LLM tools |
| BENCHMARKS.md | Every measured number, with its command |
| examples/ledger | The demo service: sdk with the Go SDK, protocol in Julia with no SDK |
| bench | Ten planted bugs, each with a correct and a too-narrow fix |
| CONTRIBUTING.md | How to contribute (DCO sign-off required) |

## Open source

Kavach is licensed under Apache 2.0. The core replayer, the flight
recorder, the CLI and the MCP server are Apache 2.0 and will stay that way.
Any future commercial offering will be built around them, not by moving them.

Contributions are accepted under the Developer Certificate of Origin;
there is no CLA. Telemetry, if it is ever added, will be opt-in.

 How does gitby make a file read-only?

title: Show HN: OpenTaxRate – open-source US sales tax rates by street address
author: winxton
body:
I built this because I tried many sales tax APIs and the problems were:
a) the rates were a black box with no source attached
b) lookups resolved by ZIP code.ZIP codes are postal routes, not tax jurisdictions. Stripe's Tax team wrote a good post on this [1]: two houses in Drexel, MO share a city, a ZIP, and nearly a house number, but sit in different counties with different rates. If your lookup key is the ZIP, you are wrong on those addresses, even when the rate table is accurate.OpenTaxRate resolves the street address instead:
- SST member states (24): the quarterly rate + boundary files, street ranges and ZIP+4, not just the rate tables
- Non-SST states: a custom adapter for each state, using its DOR's own published tables and boundary files (TX Comptroller, FL DR-15DSS, ALDOR, IDOR, NY Pub 718, California via CDTFA's lookup, etc)
- Census TIGER for geometryI tried with multiple open source geocoders you can self-host: Nominatim, Photon and Pelias, as well as proprietary ones (HERE, Geocodio, Mapbox, Google). Proprietary ones have higher accuracy, ~99.3% correct vs. 97.1% with just open source.For comparison: Avalara AvaTax 99.6%, TaxJar 98.2%. Public benchmark set are in the repo and at opentaxrate.com/benchmarks.Rates are just one part of sales tax, but also there's a ton of work in maintaining it as rules change. It doesn't handle exemptions, holidays, and caps.It returns the rate, plus the state's own location and jurisdiction codes for the address, resolved to the address, with its official source attached. MIT licensed, you can self-host with Postgres + PostGIS.[1]: https://stripe.dev/blog/how-we-built-it-jurisdiction-resolut...

## README

# Panel

A research workspace where the agent works beside you: chat, files, PDFs and notebooks in one dock, and the agent can also create custom viewers and apps when necessary

This is an early build for testers. Expect rough edges, and feel free to raise issues.

Screenshot of Panel in action.

## Before you start

- Node 22.18 or newer (or 24.12 and newer)
- pnpm
- uv, which fetches the Python it needs (3.12 or newer) by itself
- Claude Code, installed and signed in: run `claude` once and log in. The agent and the literature review run through it.

## Install and start

```sh
pnpm install
uv sync
pnpm start
```

Then open. `pnpm start` builds the app first, so the first start takes a minute. Ctrl-C stops everything it started.

## Where your things are

- `~/Panel/panel.db` holds your conversations and everything the agents did.
- `~/Panel/workspaces` is where new Workspaces are created, unless you pick another folder.

Both are outside this folder, so deleting or re-cloning the repo keeps them.

## What works

- Chatting with an agent that can read and write files, and asks before running a tool.
- Workspaces: a folder the agent works in, with its own chats and saved layout.
- Panes for files, PDFs, markdown and Jupyter notebooks. Notebooks run against a real kernel, and you and the agent can edit the same one.
- Long-running commands in the background, which you can watch and stop.
- Panes the agent writes for you when you ask to see something a built-in Pane cannot show.
- A literature review: ask the chat for one, and open its result from the tool card.

## What doesn't yet

- Currently only has full support for Claude Code.
- Modules start only by asking the chat. There is no button to launch one.
- The hypothesis Modules have no view of their own, so their results can be hard to read.
- Modules don't work with OpenAI API yet.

## The OpenAI key (optional)

Copy `apps/server/.env.example` to `apps/server/.env` and set `OPENAI_API_KEY`. This adds "OpenAI API" to the agent picker, for chat and tools.

It does not run literature reviews or the hypothesis Modules: those need an agent that can search the web, and today only Claude Code can. Without a key, the picker shows OpenAI as not set up, which is expected.

## If something's wrong

- **"Panel couldn't reach its server."** The server half is not running. Check the terminal `pnpm start` is in, then press Retry.
- **An agent shows as not set up.** The reason is written under the message box.
- **A port is already in use**, or the app answers but never loads: run `pnpm dev:doctor`. It says what is holding each port and how to clear it.

## Licence

MIT

---

## The idea

### UI

The UI has multiple configurable windows, called Panes, that can display things ranging from image files, data files, code, as well as chat sessions. This is critical for researchers who often have to context switch between different types of files.

A default set of Panes are provided for common use cases. But custom Panes can also be added by humans and agents, such as a PDB viewer or SQLite visualizer.

### Module Protocol

Modules are similar to Skills but with additional definitions to support inter-module workflows and integration with the workspace.

Specifically, Modules have typed definitions for Inputs, Outputs, and Intermediates.

Inputs and Outputs are straightforward. Intermediates refer to objects that provide observability, such as the Chain-of-Thought or scratchpad for an agentic Module, or may be intermediate outputs in a multi-stage Module. These are especially important for processes that need transparency or long-running jobs that should show progress.

Having typed definitions for these enable validation at runtime and make it easier for humans and agents to develop custom Modules for downstream tasks and Panes for visualizations.

#### Data Abstraction Layer

A data abstraction layer (DAL) bridges in-memory and filesystem objects. A DAL helps to map a URI to either an in-memory store or a local file, so that the Module just has to concern itself with the manipulation of the object.

## README

# livediff

Stay on top of what your coding agents are doing with a live diff feed, right in
your terminal.

`livediff` watches the current Git repository and shows every edit as it happens,
whether it comes from an agent, an editor, or another tool. Changes appear like a
regular Git diff: added lines are green, removed lines are red, and unchanged
lines provide context. Each edit is shown once, keeping the feed focused on what
your agents are changing now.

## Install

Run this in your terminal:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stagas/livediff/main/install.sh | sh
```

The installer supports Linux and macOS on x64 or ARM64, and Windows x64 through
Git Bash. It downloads a standalone executable; only Git needs to be installed.

## Get started

Open a terminal in any Git repository and run:

```sh
livediff
```

Now edit and save a file. You will see output similar to:

```diff
diff --git a/example.ts b/example.ts 3:47:12 PM
--- a/example.ts
+++ b/example.ts
@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
-const greeting = "Hello";
+const greeting = "Hello, world!";
```

Only edits made after `livediff` starts are displayed. It watches tracked files
and new files that are not excluded by your Git ignore rules.

Press `q` or Ctrl-C to stop.

## Compact mode

For a quieter view with only the filename, time, and changed lines, run:

```sh
livediff --compact
```

The short form works too:

```sh
livediff -c
```

Compact output looks like this:

```diff
example.ts 3:47:12 PM
-const greeting = "Hello";
+const greeting = "Hello, world!";
```

## Color and install location

Disable colors when redirecting output or using a terminal without color support:

```sh
NO_COLOR=1 livediff
```

The installer uses `/usr/local/bin` when it is writable and `~/.local/bin`
otherwise. To choose a different directory:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stagas/livediff/main/install.sh | INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/bin" sh
```

Release checksums are available as `SHA256SUMS` on the GitHub Releases page.

## Development

The project uses Go. To test or compile it from source:

```sh
go test ./...
go build -o dist/livediff .
```

author: ac-ciano

# ordewell/ordewell

Multi-agent task orchestration for coding agents. Turn one goal into an ordered plan of tasks — each with its own runner, model and mode — then execute and verify the results.

- Stars: 4
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 4
- Open issues: 0
- License: Other
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-07-31T15:20:40Z

## Languages

- CSS
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Shell
- TypeScript

## Top Contributors

- ac-ciano (10 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 Turn one goal into an ordered plan of coding-agent tasks — each with its own runner, model and mode — then execute and verify it. 
 

 
 Website ·
 Docs 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

---

## What this is

- **A plan you can rewrite before a token is spent.** The plan is a typed artifact, not an agent's internal state: every task carries a runner, model, thinking effort and mode, and you can change any of them, add and remove tasks, and rewire dependencies — without losing completed work or round-tripping the AI.
- **The right model per task, chosen in the open.** The planner makes one portfolio decision across the whole plan — a security refactor and a README update do not deserve the same model — and shows you every assignment before anything runs (why a separate planner?).
- **Verdicts from evidence, not opinion.** A task completes only when its unique completion marker appears in the runner's output; exit code is retained as diagnostic evidence. The model is never the tie-breaker. Stuck tasks can be advanced with *Mark complete*, and a task marked done by mistake goes back with *Mark not done*.
- **A planner that talks back.** Planning is one continuous chat: it researches your repo read-only, asks when your goal is vague, and its final message *is* the plan (ADR-0002). Reads run in parallel; anything reaching outside the workspace asks once; commands that would write are refused outright (ADR-0008).
- **No extra API key required.** Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode can *be* the planner, strictly read-only, on the subscription you already hold for the runners (ADR-0009).
- **Multi-runner by design.** Enable several and the planner assigns one per task. Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode ship built-in; anything else — Aider, your own CLI — is a plugin manifest, not a code change.

---

## Quick Start

Node.js ≥ 20 on macOS, Linux or Windows. The TUI also needs **tmux** — see
Platform support below.

```bash
npm install -g ordewell
ordewell                                       # the TUI — chat on the left, plan on the right
```

That's it. First run asks for a planner and a runner, set from inside
(`/planner`, `/runners`, `/key`) — no restart, no API key required up front.

`npx ordewell` works the same without a global install; the package also
ships scoped as `@ordewell/cli`.

For VS Code instead, install the extension — it carries its own core, so
there is nothing to install from npm:

```bash
code --install-extension ordewell.ordewell
```

Or search **Ordewell** in the Extensions view.

Building from source:
`git clone https://github.com/ordewell/ordewell.git && cd ordewell && npm install && npm run build && npm link -w packages/cli`
— see CONTRIBUTING.md.

### Scriptable / headless

Every slash command is also a subcommand — set the planner and runner by env
var to skip the TUI entirely.

**Already run Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode?** No separate API key — it
runs on the subscription you already hold:

```bash
export AI_PROVIDER="claude-code"        # or codex, opencode
ordewell plan --goal "Add rate limiting to the public API" && ordewell run
```

Mutation always stays with the runners; the planner agent only explores and
reasons. Same toggles apply from a UI: `/planner`, `/model`,
`/planner-effort`, or the planner bar in VS Code.

**Prefer an API key?** Twenty-five providers are recognised via their own
`*_API_KEY` — OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, xAI, Groq, DeepSeek,
Mistral, Together, Fireworks, Perplexity, Cerebras, DeepInfra, Cohere,
Novita, Kimi, Zhipu, Qwen, Doubao, Hunyuan, Baichuan, MiniMax, Yi, StepFun
and SiliconFlow. Run `ordewell key` for variable names, or point
`OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_BASE_URL` at anything else, including a local model
server.

```bash
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="sk-or-..."
ordewell plan --goal "Add rate limiting to the public API" && ordewell run
```

---

## Three surfaces, one core

### VS Code

A streaming timeline: live thinking, each research step with its outcome, and task cards you expand for the runner's own output. Retarget a task's runner and its model and mode re-derive in place. The whole loop is below, under **The VS Code loop, end to end**.

### Terminal UI

 

Everything the extension does, over SSH. `tab` swaps chat and plan pane; single keys drive the plan (`f` start, `E` run all, `m` toggle done, `R` runner, `o` model). `/help` lists the rest.

### CLI

```console
$ ordewell plan --goal "Add rate limiting to the public API"

Generating plan for: "Add rate limiting to the public API"...
✓ list_dir src → D middleware F router.ts F auth.ts
✓ grep X-RateLimit → no matches in 6 files

Question: should limits apply per API key, or per client IP?
My recommendation: per key — auth() already threads the key through req.ctx.
> per key, with an IP fallback for anonymous routes

Plan: 4 tasks (3 AI, 1 Manual) — claude-code, opencode
Session: session-1751600000000

   1. [ AI] Add a token-bucket limiter in src/middleware/rateLimit.ts (Claude Sonnet 4.5 · Claude Code)
   2. [ AI] Wire the limiter into route registration (Claude Haiku 4.5 · Claude Code)
   3. [ AI] Return RFC 6585 429s with Retry-After (DeepSeek V4 Flash · Opencode)
   4. [MAN] Document the limit headers in the OpenAPI spec

  [MAN] = manual step — run `ordewell tui` to work through it

  Run 'ordewell run' to execute, 'ordewell status' to inspect, or 'ordewell tui' for the full UI.

$ ordewell run
Executing plan...
  ✓ #a1b2 completed — PASS: Verified: completion marker detected in agent output. Task c
  ⟳ #c3d4 in_progress
[2/Wire the limiter into route registration] Started: claude-code / claude-haiku-4-5

Done. 4 completed, 0 failed, 0 blocked.
```

Every slash command is also an `ordewell` subcommand, so nothing is UI-only and headless automation reaches everything a human can.

---

## How it works

1. **Describe a goal** in plain prose.
2. **The planner researches** your workspace read-only and interleaves questions with research in one persistent conversation (ADR-0008).
3. **A plan appears** — ordered tasks, each with a runner, model, thinking effort and mode. Edit anything inline, or reprompt to reshape the whole plan without losing completed work.
4. **Execution** spawns a real coding-agent session per AI task, respecting the dependency graph and handing each task its predecessors' results. Manual tasks become checklists.
5. **The VerdictEngine** completes a task only once its marker appears; an exit without one fails visibly. Sessions auto-save to `.ordewell/sessions/`.

---

 
 Usage examples — planning, editing, multi-runner, plugins 

**Plan, edit, execute**

```bash
# The planner researches the repo and converses if the goal is underspecified
ordewell plan --goal "Migrate the config loader from JSON to TOML"

# Reassign before running — runner first, since it re-derives model, effort and mode
ordewell task-runner 2 opencode
ordewell task-deps 3 1,2

# Execute; independent tasks run in parallel (default: 3 concurrent sessions)
ordewell run

# Inspect any session later
ordewell status --session-id session-1751600000000
```

The surfaces differ only in how you name a target: the TUI opens a picker, the CLI takes an argument — and omitting the argument prints the same options the picker would have shown.

```bash
ordewell task-model 3            # lists the models that task's runner can spawn
ordewell task-model 3 sonnet     # picks one
```

**Configure without an editor**

```bash
ordewell planner claude-code     # plan on a coding agent's subscription — no API key
ordewell model set sonnet        # scoped to that agent's own catalog
ordewell planner-effort high     # a variant of the selected model
ordewell key set openrouter sk-… # stored in .env, never echoed back
ordewell runners codex off
```

Each pushes to the running server *before* writing `.env`, so the change lands on the next plan with no restart — and a refused connection cannot leave the file holding a setting the daemon never saw.

**Deep-interview planning with a PRD**

```bash
ordewell grill-me on   # planner interrogates your goal before outlining (min. 3 probing questions)
ordewell prd on        # planner previews, then writes a full PRD to .scratch/<slug>/PRD.md
ordewell tdd on        # tasks are augmented with red-green-refactor instructions

ordewell plan --goal "Real-time collaborative editing"
# → the planner grills you in chat, drafts the PRD, waits for your OK,
#   then commits the plan as its final message
```

**Multi-runner plans and custom runners**

```bash
# Pass --runner repeatedly to build a runner set; the planner assigns one per task
ordewell plan --goal "Refactor auth module" --runner claude-code --runner opencode

# Bring your own CLI agent via a plugin manifest
ordewell plugins create my-runner        # scaffolds manifest.json
ordewell plugins install github:user/repo
ordewell plugins list
```

**The other two front ends**

```bash
ordewell               # full-screen terminal UI — same as `ordewell tui`
ordewell web --daemon  # the local API server, in the background
```

`ordewell web` starts the HTTP + WebSocket API on `127.0.0.1:3742` that the CLI and TUI are clients of — every other command starts it for you on demand. It serves JSON, not a web page; there is no browser dashboard yet.

For VS Code, install the extension and open the Ordewell panel — see Quick Start.

| Area | Commands |
| --- | --- |
| Planning | type a goal, `/approve`, `/run`, `/stop` |
| Tasks | `/add-task`, `/remove-task`, `/complete`, `/uncomplete`, `/skip`, `/retry`, `/cancel`, `/force-start` |
| Skills | `/grill-me`, `/tdd`, `/prd`, `/review`, `/verify`, `/research-subagents` |
| Models | `/model`, `/key`, `/allowlist`, `/runners`, `/auto`, `/refresh` |
| Sessions | `/sessions`, `/new`, `/save`, `/load`, `/delete` — a loaded session is adopted by the server, so its plan stays executable |
| System | `/help`, `/mouse`, `/quit` |

API keys typed into `/key` are masked on screen and written to your `.env`.

Text is selectable and copyable with the mouse, as in any other program: Ordewell
does not capture the terminal's mouse. Scroll with `pgup`/`pgdn`. If you would
rather have wheel scrolling and can live without drag-to-select, `/mouse on`
swaps the trade (and remembers it via `ORDEWELL_TUI_MOUSE` in your `.env`).

A task's own terminal is a tmux window, where tmux does hold the mouse so the
wheel scrolls its scrollback. Selecting there still copies to your system
clipboard: drag to select and release to copy, or double/triple-click for a word
or a line. Install `wl-copy`, `xclip` or `xsel` on Linux if you have none of them
— without one, copying falls back to an OSC 52 escape that some terminals ignore.

 

 
 The VS Code loop, end to end — research, question, plan, execution, verdict 

 

 

 
 Platform support — including the Windows notes 

| Surface | Linux | macOS | Windows |
|---------|-------|-------|---------|
| VS Code extension | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| API server | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| CLI | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| TUI | ✅ needs tmux | ✅ needs tmux | needs tmux — run it under WSL |

**The TUI requires tmux on every platform**, not only Windows — it is what backs
each task's live terminal. Install it from your package manager (`apt install
tmux`, `brew install tmux`) before running `ordewell`. Everything else runs
natively on Windows: the planner (including harness planners), task execution,
model discovery, and the read-only exploration envelope all work there.

Two notes for Windows. Install the agent CLIs with their **native installers** where one exists — an npm-installed `claude`/`codex`/`opencode` is a `.cmd` shim, which has to start through cmd.exe and inherits its 8191-character command-line limit; that is fine for task prompts but not for the harness planner's larger system prompt, and Ordewell will tell you so by name rather than silently truncating it. And keep **Git for Windows** installed: its POSIX shell is what the planner runs research commands in, so `ls`, `cat`, `grep` and friends behave the same as they do everywhere else. See ADR-0010.

Any install route is found, on PATH or not: the PowerShell one-liner installers (`irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex`, OpenCode's equivalent), npm, pnpm, Yarn, bun, Scoop, Chocolatey, WinGet, and Volta. If a runner is greyed out in the picker right after you installed it, restart the VS Code window — a GUI-launched extension host holds the PATH it started with.

 

 
 Configuration — the four settings that matter 

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One provider key (`OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, …) | — | The one required setting. Twenty-five providers are recognised, each from its own variable — `ordewell key` lists them — plus any OpenAI-compatible endpoint via `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_BASE_URL`. The provider is auto-detected from whichever key is set (force with `AI_PROVIDER`). Not needed when `AI_PROVIDER` is `claude-code`, `codex`, or `opencode` — those plan with the CLI's own subscription. |
| `ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL` | `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` | The planner model — a budget model by default; it plans and researches but never writes code. Change via `ordewell model set ` or `/model`, which scope the choice to the planner backend's own catalog. With a coding-agent planner, it must be one of that agent's own model ids. |
| `ORDEWELL_PLANNER_EFFORT` | — | Thinking effort for a coding-agent planner, from the selected model's own variants (`low`, `high`, `adaptive`, …). Ignored by vendor planners, whose effort is baked into the model id. Change via `ordewell planner-effort ` or `/planner-effort`. |
| `ORDEWELL_MAX_PARALLEL` | `3` | Max concurrent AI task sessions (1–5). Independent tasks run in parallel; the dependency graph is always respected. |

Run `ordewell --help` for the full list of environment variables, or `ordewell setup` for the interactive wizard. VS Code users: everything is mirrored under `ordewell.*` settings.

 

 
 Architecture 

```text
packages/
├── core/    Pure TypeScript, zero UI deps — Session, PlanStore, Planner,
│            TaskOrchestrator, VerdictEngine, ModelResolver, ModeResolver,
│            RunnerRegistry + manifest template engine
├── cli/     ordewell: tui, plan, run, status, stop, web, models, setup,
│            plugins, grill-me, prd, tdd — plus tui/, a pure state +
│            renderer core behind a thin raw-mode terminal driver
├── vscode/  Extension + webview: streaming planner timeline, task cards,
│            TTY capture via script(1)
└── web/     Hono HTTP + WebSocket server — the local daemon the CLI and
             TUI drive over 127.0.0.1 (session pool, headless execution)
```

The TUI's core is pure — a reducer returning `{ state, effects }` and a renderer returning one string per terminal row (ADR-0006).

Tasks default to each runner's autonomous mode (toggle with `/auto`), and the plan is the source of truth for what runs — modes are never silently rewritten at spawn (ADR-0001).

Every surface consumes one event union (`SessionMessage`) over one broadcast seam — the domain vocabulary lives in CONTEXT.md and design decisions in docs/adr/.

 

 
 Acknowledgements 

The deep-interview planning workflows — `grill-me`, PRD drafting, TDD task augmentation, and review mode — are adapted from Matt Pocock's skills (MIT), rebuilt as prompt blocks inside Ordewell's planner and runner prompts. If you want those workflows in a plain coding-agent session rather than an orchestrated plan, his repo is the place to start.

 

---

## Contributing

Bug reports, feature requests and pull requests are welcome — start with CONTRIBUTING.md for the build order and the layout of the tree. Security issues go to SECURITY.md, not the public tracker.

New to the codebase? CONTEXT.md is the domain glossary and docs/adr/ records why things are the way they are.

---

## README

# fugleramme
E-ink bird frame for Raspberry Pi - real-time bird detection by audio.

Built on top of BirdNET-Go, which runs
the mic and the BirdNET classifier and owns all detection config. Fugleramme reads
its detections and renders the recently-seen birds as a collage on an Inky-Impression e-ink panel, and serves the same view as a web kiosk.

## Art

The birds are cut-outs from historic, public-domain natural-history drawings,
hand-curated for this project. Each detected species is matched to its
illustration, background-removed, and packed onto a textured paper page - larger
birds toward the centre, sized by real body mass. Species with no illustration
are currently left off, and an empty window shows a bare perch.

| No detections | A few visitors | A full garden |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| No birds detected | A few garden birds | Many garden birds |

## Run locally

```bash
uv sync                                       # set up venv
uv run python -m fugleramme.seed --count 40   # seed db (no BirdNET-Go in dev)
uv run fugleramme-frame                       # start service on :8080
uv run fugleramme-dev                         # same as above with hot-reload
```

Open the kiosk (no SPI-panel needed):

```bash
open -na "Google Chrome" --args --kiosk --app=http://localhost:8080/
```

## Run on a Raspberry Pi

Clone the repo on the Pi and run the idempotent one-command bootstrap:

```bash
./setup.sh          # add -y to auto-accept dependency installs (uv, docker, etc...)
```

It installs any missing deps, brings up BirdNET-Go (container + mic), and enables
the frame as a systemd service that pushes to the Inky panel and serves the kiosk
on `:8080`. Details: `detector/README.md`. 

Want to update? Just pull and run ./setup.sh again

## License

- Code (`wikimedia-scrape/`, application code): MIT - see `LICENSE`.
- Bird images (`assets/birds/`): CC BY-SA 4.0 - see
 `assets/birds/ATTRIBUTION.md`.
- Bird sizes (`assets/bird_sizes.csv`): body mass from AVONET (Tobias et al.
 2022, Ecology Letters, doi:10.1111/ele.13898),
 CC BY 4.0.

A mic listens to the sounds in my garden, BirdNET-Go (an open-source BirdNET classifier) detects birds by sound, and the e-ink frame draws a real 1800s natural-history illustration of each one as it hears them. Here’s a live web-demo from my garden in Bergen, Norway: https://fugleramme.arnegiacomo.devA few things that might be interesting:- The screen only redraws when the set of birds changes, and dithers the collage down to six colours for the e-ink display.- Bigger birds sit toward the centre, scaled by real body mass.- 800+ cutouts across 400+ species, each cut from a real public domain plate. All art is historic and human-made. Coverage is currently best for the Nordics, Britain and Germany (but other parts of the world are in the works).- Runs fully local on a Raspberry Pi or your homelab (yes, even the classifier runs great on a RPI)The e-ink panel is optional and it can run web-only in a container against a BirdNET-Go you already have.Happy to answer any questions!

Author here: Fair, i could've been more explicit in my writing. Concretely:Every bird is a cutout from a real scanned 1800s plate (Gould, the von Wright

comments.text: There are LLMs that support audio input, similar to those with vision support.From my testing of open weights LLMs with audio support, they basically are only trained to recognize audio as an alternative to text input, they treat audio as basically equivalent to a transcript, and can't recognize or distinguish things like music, accents, background sounds, etc.So they're only really good for transcribing or summarizing or using audio input in place of text input for prompts, but not anything that requires distinguishing any information about the audio that would not be present in a transcript.It can be tempting to try to use an LLM for a variety of tasks; kind of the whole thing about an LLM is that you don't have to do a separate complex training run for every task, but can just provide instructions in natural language. But it only works as far as what the training data covers, if the training basically always treated audio and a text transcript as equivalent, the model has nothing causing it to learn other relevant features of the audio. If there's enough bird call identification in the training data of an LLM, it might be able to do that, but I think multimodal training data tends to be much more limited than the text training corpus

title: Show HN: Breathe CLI – Paced resonance breathing in the macOS terminal
author: marekkowalczyk
body: I built a terminal app that paces slow breathing at 6 breaths per minute for vagal tone training. It's a single Python file, stdlib only, no dependencies — just run breathe and follow the bar.I'm a cardiology patient (HFrEF). Slow breathing at resonance frequency is one of the few non-pharmacological interventions shown to improve cardiac vagal tone and baroreflex sensitivity (Bernardi et al., Circulation 2002; Lancet 1998). I wanted a frictionless daily habit tool — no app store, no account, no subscription, just open terminal and go.Design constraints, all grounded in the clinical literature:- No breath retention — Valsalva risk in cardiac patients- No rapid breathing — minimum 8-second cycles- Exhale ≤ 2x inhale — no evidence for extreme ratios- Immediate exit, always — q or Ctrl+C restores the terminal even on crashThe README includes a resonance frequency measurement protocol for anyone with a chest-strap HRV monitor who wants to find their individual optimum instead of using the 6 bpm default.macOS only (uses afplay for audio cues). MIT licensed.pip install breathe-cliorbrew tap marekkowalczyk/breathe && brew install breathe.

title: Show HN: Jynx, a matchmaking app to find gaming teammates
author: akiro____
body:
TL;DR: Jynx is a gaming social platform that matches you with compatible teammates based on skill level, play style and schedule. Swipe to find players (Tinder-style), create or join game sessions (LFG), chat, and build your squad. 214k lines of Dart, 23 feature modules, built entirely with Claude Code as my entry into agentic engineering.Live on App Store and Play Store:
https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=app.jynx
https://apps.apple.com/fr/app/jynx-where-gaming-gets-social/...---Hi HN, long time lurker, first time poster, be gentle.Developer by day, vibe coder by night: Jynx is the project I used to ease into agentic engineering.AI talks are mitigated, at best. But I'll talk about my experience here. Forgive my erratic style, it is what it is.Working with Claude from the very beginning, it's been a blast. I had the "chance" to have the time necessary to learn and use AI a lot. Lots of different techniques that quickly became completely obsolete today.Without LLMs, it would have been extremely hard to have the same app than I have today. I used Flutter (Dart) to avoid having to dev and maintain two codebases. It is not a language I knew. Learning the language first would have severely hindered the process.For me, from copy/paste to using MCP then Roo Code, then Claude Code was an ecstatic process. I always loved having ideas but the time it would take me to build the thing and test it always felt too long. Not anymore.So we carefully designed, iterated and implemented the two codebases for Jynx. One for the flutter app, one for the firebase backend. I chose Firebase to avoid having to maintain a server and be able to focus on the UI/UX of the app.We started thinking about it in December 2024 and started devs early 2025; not working on it full time at all. We really poured our heart into it and we truly tried to make it as secure as possible. Even though we mean business, it is a passion project. By using the excuse of learning agentic flows, I took the time to inspect each aspects of the app's systems thoroughly.Tech stack:
- Flutter 3.41 / Dart 3.11 (single codebase, iOS + Android)
- Firebase (Firestore, Cloud Functions in TypeScript, Auth, Storage, FCM)
- Riverpod 3.1 + Freezed + json_serializable for state management & immutable models
- Drift for encrypted local SQLite caching (offline-first architecture to optimize Firebase costs)
- Clean Architecture with feature modules and mixin-based repositories
- Sentry + Firebase Crashlytics for production error reporting
- Freerasp for runtime app self-protection (tamper detection, root/jailbreak)Agentic engineering artifacts:
- Claude Code (Claude + GLM) as primary coding agent
- 22 hooks, 18 skills, 13 instincts, 8 rule files, custom subagents, slash commands, MCP servers and plugins (instincts system from Affaan's https://github.com/affaan-m/everything-claude-code)
- GitNexus
- MemPalace for persistent context across sessionsStats: 1,239 Dart files, 214k lines of code (excluding generated boilerplate), 30k lines of comments across the Flutter codebase.I made a detailed cheatsheet document about my whole setup if you want it. I could post it or you DM me.If you have questions, ask away, I'll gladly answer.Test it and tell me what you think of it honestly, I won't get offended!Take care,
Antoine

## README

# turboGPT

Tiny byte-level GPT training in CUDA C++. MIT.

## Build

Linux/NixOS:

```bash
nix-build -o build/nix-result
```

Windows, Visual Studio 2022 C++ tools, and CUDA 13.4:

```powershell
.\build.ps1 -CudaArch 86
```

`CudaArch` is the GPU compute capability from NVIDIA's CUDA GPU list.

## Run

```powershell
.\build\turbogpt.exe --data hn1g.txt --log-to runs/ctx4
```

The run stores its checkpoint at
`runs/ctx4/ctx4.pt`, containing model, optimizer, scheduler, and trainer state.
Use `--load CHECKPOINT.pt` to resume it.

`runs/ctx4/report.json` is derived from the log directory. Logs are TensorBoard-compatible:
one report per batch, capped at 8Mi reports, and flushed with periodic or final checkpoints.

## Result

- hn1g after 1.5G training tokens: **2.5295 BPB**.

## Tests

```powershell
python tests\verify.py
```
